title: Robust Quantum Memory Advantage from Contextuality
abstract: Quantum contextuality is widely recognized as an essential non-classical resource underlying quantum technology, yet illuminating the precise mechanisms through which it translates into unconditional computational advantages remains an ongoing challenge. We demonstrate an exponential, noise-resilient memory advantage for quantum finite automata arising from graph-theoretic approaches to contextuality. We define a promise problem on an exclusivity graph $G$ for which any classical deterministic automaton acts as a non-contextual hidden variable model requiring at least $N=χ(G)$ states, where $χ(G)$ is the graph's chromatic number. In contrast, by exploiting a structural phenomenon we term \textit{representational contextuality}, a QFA solves this task using a memory of dimension at most $d=ξ(G)+1$, where $ξ(G)$ is the graph's orthogonal rank. This separation scales exponentially ($d=\mathcal O(n)$ versus $N=2^{Ω(n)}$) for Boolean-orthogonality graphs. Crucially, this memory advantage maintains an $\mathcal{O}(1)$ threshold against both depolarizing and coherent noise.
summary: The paper proves an unconditional exponential memory advantage of Quantum Finite Automata over classical automata by exploiting graph-theoretic contextuality. By analyzing the Kochen-Specker Problem on specific graphs, it shows that the required quantum memory scales linearly with system size ($\xi(G)$), while the classical requirement scales exponentially ($\chi(G)$). This advantage is robust to common types of noise.
main_problem: The paper aims to demonstrate an exponential, noise-resilient memory advantage for quantum finite automata (QFAs) over classical deterministic finite automata (DFAs) by leveraging the structural resource of quantum contextuality.
main_result: An exponential separation is shown between the classical state requirement ($\chi(G)$) and the quantum memory dimension ($\xi(G)+1$) needed to solve a promise problem derived from the Kochen-Specker Problem (KSP).
method: The analysis uses graph theory invariants—the chromatic number $\chi(G)$ and orthogonal rank $\xi(G)$—to establish bounds on classical vs. quantum memory resources for recognizing specific logical structures.
model_or_system: The core model is the comparison between DFAs and QFAs solving a promise problem defined on an exclusivity graph $G$. The advantage is demonstrated using Boolean-orthogonality graphs ($\Omega_n$) or Kochen-Specker graphs derived from high-dimensional polytopes.
key_observables: Classical memory cost ($N = \chi(G)$) versus Quantum memory dimension ($d = \xi(G)+1$).
important_parameters: The exponential scaling difference between $\chi(G)$ and $\xi(G)$, and the maintenance of an $O(1)$ noise threshold against depolarizing/coherent noise.
main_assumptions: The advantage relies on 'representational contextuality,' defined by the integer gap $\chi(G) > \xi(G)$, which is a stronger condition than statistical contextuality ($\chi_f(G)$).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the graph structures (e.g., $\Omega_4$, 18-vertex graph, 60-ray orthogonality graph) and compare the exponential scaling of classical memory cost versus the linear scaling of quantum memory cost.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the problem using KSP on a graph $G$. It then proves the lower bound for DFAs ($\chi(G)$). Subsequently, it constructs the QFA solution using $\xi(G)+1$ dimensions and rigorously demonstrates the exponential separation and noise resilience.
why_interesting: This work provides concrete, quantifiable bounds showing how structural quantum resources (contextuality) translate into computational advantages that are robust against realistic physical noise models, which is crucial for building fault-tolerant quantum computation.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The complete Boolean-orthogonality graph Ω4. Vertices are colored such that no two connected vertices share a color, illustrating that χ(Ω4) = 4.

Figure 2: Scaling of the state space dimension as a function of the graph dimension n. While the quantum memory cost ξ(Ωn) (blue) grows linearly, the lower bound on the classical memory cost χ(Ωn) (red dashed), derived from the Frankl-Rodl (FR) theorem [35], grows exponentially.

Figure 3: This 18-vertex graph has χ = 7, ξ = 6 and χf = 5.68. It cannot exhibit state- independent contextuality because χf < ξ [18]. However, it does exhibit representational contextuality, as χ > ξ.

Figure 4: A valid 6-coloring of the 60-ray orthogonality graph of [42] derived from vertices of the 4D 600-cell. The graph is partitioned into 15 disjoint 4-element orthogonal bases (indicated by the shaded regions). Because each basis forms a clique, every region contains four distinct vertex colors.
